overview: Alliant Energy is a regulated investor-owned electric and natural gas utility holding company headquartered in Madison, Wisconsin, operating through two public utility subsidiaries: Interstate Power and Light (IPL, serving ~505,000 electric and ~230,000 gas customers in Iowa) and Wisconsin Power and Light (WPL, serving ~505,000 electric and ~205,000 gas customers in Wisconsin). The company earns a regulated return on an expanding rate base built from renewable generation, natural gas, energy storage and grid investments, supplemented by a small non-utility segment (AEF) holding transmission (ATC), a leased gas-fired facility, and a freight/logistics business (Travero).

business_model.summary: Alliant earns cost-of-service regulated returns on rate base at IPL (Iowa, regulated by the IUC) and WPL (Wisconsin, regulated by the PSCW). Revenue grows primarily through rate case-approved base rate increases tied to capital investment (generation, distribution, renewables) and through retail/wholesale volume growth, with a growing contribution from large-load data center customers on individual contract rates. A small non-utility holding company (AEF) and a 16-20% stake in American Transmission Company (ATC) contribute supplemental, largely non-regulated/FERC-regulated earnings.

revenue_streams.name: Non-utility / AEF (Travero, Sheboygan Falls lease, venture investments)

business_model.customer_type: Residential, commercial and industrial retail utility customers in Iowa and Wisconsin, plus a small and rapidly growing base of large-load/data-center customers on individual contract rates, and wholesale municipal/cooperative customers
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% Midwest U.S. - Iowa (IPL) and Wisconsin (WPL); FY2025 total revenue ~$4.2B split roughly evenly between IPL (~$2.16B) and WPL (~$2.06B)

main_competitors: MidAmerican Energy Company (Berkshire Hathaway Energy, Iowa)
competitive_position.market_position: Exclusive franchised monopoly electric and gas distributor within its Iowa and Wisconsin service territories; mid-cap regulated utility (~$20B market cap range) competing for large-load/data-center siting decisions against neighboring utilities and self-generation alternatives

moat_factors.description: Retail electric and gas customers in Iowa and Wisconsin cannot choose their utility; IPL and WPL have the exclusive obligation and right to serve, eliminating direct retail competition

Capital investment earns a regulator-authorized return on equity (IPL ~9.3-11.25% by asset class; WPL ~9.8% for 2026/2027), providing predictable, recurring earnings growth tied to the ~$13.4-15.9B multi-year capex plan
Generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure requires massive capital and decades-long regulatory approvals (GCU Certificates, CPCNs), effectively blocking new entrants

moat_factors.factor: First-mover position on data center siting
moat_factors.description: Development-ready, rail-served industrial sites and already-executed ~3.4 GW of data center service agreements give Alliant an early lead in capturing hyperscale load growth versus neighboring utilities

weaknesses: No true retail competition insulates revenue but also means growth is capped by what regulators allow into rate base and authorized ROE
WPL lacks an automatic retail electric fuel cost adjustment clause, creating commodity cost-recovery lag risk
Revenue growth increasingly concentrated in a small number of large data-center customers, raising counterparty and demand-volatility risk
Credit ratings (BBB+/Baa2 at the parent) are mid-investment-grade, and heavy reliance on debt and equity issuance to fund growth increases interest-rate and dilution sensitivity
Two reportable utility segments depend on separate state regulators (IUC, PSCW) with different rate mechanisms, adding regulatory complexity

growth_drivers: Data center / large-load growth: ~3.4 GW of contracted demand across five executed agreements (IPL and WPL), with a further 2-4 GW of potential pipeline load; management expects peak electric demand to rise ~60% by 2031
Raised 2027-2030 capital plan of $15.9 billion (up 19% from prior plan), funding ~1,600 MW of new gas, ~1,000 MW of energy storage and ~1,300 MW of renewables plus distribution/grid modernization
Individual customer rate tariffs for large-load customers (approved in IPL's and pending at WPL's rate cases) allow new load to be priced to recover associated infrastructure costs
Long-term EPS growth target of at least 8% annually through 2030, well above the typical regulated-utility 5-7% range, driven by the data-center-driven rate base expansion
Renewable tax credit monetization (IRA transferability) - $285 million of tax credit sale proceeds in 2025 - lowering customer costs and supporting cash flow, though at risk from OBBB Act phase-outs
DOE Office of Energy Dominance Financing conditional loan guarantee commitments (~$1.4B IPL, ~$1.6B WPL) for low-cost financing of eligible generation projects
IPL's retail electric base rate moratorium (extended through 2029/2030) provides multi-year rate certainty that supports predictable earnings even as rate base grows

business.description: A small number of hyperscale customers now represent a large share of expected load growth; contracts may be delayed, reduced, or cancelled due to changing business needs, technology efficiency gains, or construction delays, and large capital is committed ahead of realizing returns
Local moratorium proposals in Iowa (e.g., Linn County) and Wisconsin driven by land use, water and noise concerns could delay or block siting and associated infrastructure cost recovery
Electric and gas sales are weather-dependent; mild winters/summers reduce volumes and cash flow

Large pipeline of generation, storage and distribution projects (Bobcat Energy Center, new wind/storage) exposed to permitting delays, cost overruns, supply chain and tariff-driven input cost inflation

financial.description: Consolidated debt-to-capitalization ~59-62%; growth plan requires continuous external financing including up to $2.4B of new common equity issuance 2026-2029, creating dilution and refinancing risk

Rising rates increase financing costs for a capital-intensive, debt-funded growth plan and increase pension/OPEB obligations; a 100bp rate increase would raise annual pre-tax expense by only ~$2M directly on variable debt, but refinancing fixed debt at higher rates is a larger ongoing drag
Mid-investment-grade ratings (BBB+/Baa2 parent) could be downgraded if credit metrics weaken, raising borrowing costs and collateral requirements

regulatory.description: IPL and WPL must obtain timely, adequate rate relief from the IUC and PSCW to earn authorized ROE; moratoriums, earnings sharing mechanisms, and investment caps (e.g., IPL's $900M/$325M-per-year electric distribution cap) can limit recoverable investment or depress realized ROE

regulatory.risk: Clean energy tax credit rollback (OBBB Act)
regulatory.description: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act accelerates termination of production/investment tax credits and restricts credits tied to foreign-sourced components, potentially reducing renewable tax credit monetization and raising customer costs
EPA rules on GHG, CCR, effluent limits and NSPS are in flux (several proposed repeals pending in 2026), creating compliance cost and coal-retirement timing uncertainty

Rising seasonal capacity planning reserve margins (up to 42% in winter) and the upcoming Direct Loss of Load capacity accreditation methodology could force additional, potentially unrecovered, capacity investment

macro.description: Tariffs, labor and materials inflation raise construction costs that may not be fully or timely recovered in rates
Growth strategy depends on continuous access to debt and equity markets; disruption (Fed policy, sovereign debt concerns, market volatility) could raise cost of capital or limit funding availability

macro_factors.industry_outlook: U.S. regulated utility sector outlook has improved materially due to AI/data-center-driven electricity demand growth after two decades of flat load; Midwest utilities with available land, transmission capacity and large-load siting programs are seeing accelerated rate base growth opportunities
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low - regulated utility demand is largely non-cyclical/defensive, though industrial/data-center load adds some sensitivity to broader economic and tech-capex cycles
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - capital-intensive, debt- and equity-funded growth model makes cost of capital a key driver of achievable ROE spreads and EPS growth
key_input_costs: Renewable equipment (wind/solar/storage, exposed to tariffs and foreign-sourcing tax credit restrictions)

recent_developments.event: Q3 2026 earnings: GAAP EPS $1.52 (vs $1.09 prior year, +39%); nine-month ongoing EPS $2.99 (+14%); narrowed 2026 ongoing EPS guidance to $3.41-$3.46 (from $3.36-$3.46)

Raised 2027-2030 capital plan 19% to $15.9 billion, with ~$6.8B to thermal generation/LNG infrastructure and ~$5.1B to renewables and storage; issued initial 2027 ongoing EPS guidance of $3.63-$3.73 (~8% growth) and a 2027 dividend target of $2.25/share (+5%)

Contracted data center demand reported at ~3.4 GW across five fully executed agreements (three under active construction), with an additional 2-4 GW of potential future-load pipeline; peak electric demand expected to rise ~60% by 2031

Raised 2026 retail sales growth guidance to 2-3% (from 1%) on accelerating data center and industrial demand; noted local political pushback/moratorium proposals in parts of Iowa and Wisconsin regarding data center siting
New ~370 MW hyperscale data center electric service agreement signed in Iowa, with full load ramp expected by 2030; Q1 EPS beat with guidance reaffirmed

PSCW order authorized WPL annual base rate increases of $69M (electric)/$7M (gas) effective Jan 1, 2026, plus a further $75M/$5M increase effective Jan 1, 2027, under the 2026/2027 forward-looking test period
Board approved 5% increase in targeted 2026 annual dividend to $2.14/share ($0.535 quarterly), effective February 2026
FERC authorized IPL to issue up to $2.5B of long-term debt in 2026-2027; PSCW authorized WPL to issue up to $2.8B of long-term debt in 2026-2028, supporting the expanded capital program
EPA finalized rescission of its 2009 GHG endangerment finding, adding uncertainty to the pace/need for coal retirements and emissions compliance spending

items.notes: Narrowed and moved to upper half of prior $3.36-$3.46 range after a strong Q3 beat (GAAP EPS $1.52, up 39% YoY); FY2025 GAAP EPS was $3.14
Implies ~8% growth versus the 2026 guidance midpoint; first look at FY2027
Above the typical regulated-utility 5-7% growth band, driven by data-center/large-load rate base growth; prior long-term target had been in the mid-single digits

19% increase versus the prior multi-year capital plan; ~$6.8B to thermal generation/LNG infrastructure, ~$5.1B to renewables/storage, remainder to distribution and other; annual spend ramps from ~$4.3B (2027) to ~$4.7B peak (2028)
5% increase year over year in both periods; payout ratio goal of 60-70% of consolidated earnings from continuing operations
Raised from 1% previously on accelerating data-center and industrial demand
Via at-the-market distribution agreement, Shareholder Direct Plan, and future equity offerings, to fund the expanded capital plan while preserving the balance sheet

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CEO Lisa Barton, CFO Robert Durian) attributed the Q3 beat to a larger regulated asset base, higher retail sales and equity earnings, while flagging that a favorable income tax timing benefit in Q3 is expected to reverse in Q4 with no full-year impact. Management emphasized confidence in the data-center pipeline (3.4 GW contracted, 2-4 GW additional potential) and reiterated that Iowa's retail base rate stability plan (moratorium) would be extended through 2030, providing earnings visibility even as the capital plan grows. Management also acknowledged rising local political opposition to data centers in parts of Iowa and Wisconsin but said current moratorium proposals (e.g., unincorporated Linn County) do not affect its contracted projects.

bull_case: Rare combination for a regulated utility: an 8%+ long-term EPS growth target versus the typical 5-7% peer range, driven by contracted and pipeline data-center load (3.4 GW contracted, 2-4 GW pipeline) and a $15.9B 2027-2030 capital plan

Exclusive franchise territories in Iowa and Wisconsin with constructive, multi-year regulatory outcomes (IPL rate moratorium through 2029/2030, WPL's 2026/2027 rate case settled with increases locked in for both years) provide earnings visibility

Individual customer rate tariffs let Alliant price large-load customers to recover dedicated infrastructure costs, mitigating much of the stranded-asset risk historically associated with large single-customer buildouts

Access to low-cost DOE loan guarantee commitments (~$3B combined for IPL/WPL) and IRA tax credit transferability (sold $285M of credits in 2025) help fund growth while keeping customer rates competitive
Investment-grade credit ratings (BBB+/Baa2 parent, A-/Baa1 WPL) and a stated dividend growth policy (5% increases, $2.25 target for 2027) support a total-return thesis for income-oriented investors
bear_case: Earnings growth is increasingly dependent on a handful of hyperscale data-center contracts; cancellation, delay, or lower-than-expected ramp (due to efficiency gains, siting disputes, or macro AI-capex pullback) could undercut the above-average growth narrative priced into the stock

Funding a $15.9B capital plan requires continuous heavy debt issuance plus up to $2.4B of equity issuance through 2029, creating dilution risk and leverage that is sensitive to interest rates and credit-rating actions

Local political opposition to data centers (moratorium proposals in parts of Iowa and Wisconsin) could slow or block future large-load siting and associated rate-base growth beyond already-contracted projects

Federal clean-energy tax policy (OBBB Act phase-outs of production/investment tax credits, foreign-sourcing restrictions) could raise project costs or shrink tax-credit monetization that currently funds customer bill offsets and cash flow

Regulatory risk remains structural: IUC/PSCW earnings-sharing mechanisms, rate moratoria, and investment caps (e.g., IPL's distribution spending cap) mean upside from growing rate base can be capped or clawed back if authorized ROE is exceeded
